groups.content:
Inca engineering

Mountain roads

  • [1] were cut into the rock on steep slopes.
  • Retaining [2] stopped the road from sliding down the hill.
  • [3] beside the road carried rainwater away.

Grass suspension bridges

  • The main [4] were made of braided grass cords.
  • The floor was made of [5] laid across the lowest cables.
  • Bridges were normally replaced every [6].

groups.instruction:
Questions 18-22

Complete the summary using the list of words, A-H, below.

Write the correct letter, A-H, in boxes 18-22 on your answer sheet.

A   useful
B   isolated
C   overall
D   worrying
E   recent
F   accurate
G   expensive
H   rapid
groups.content:
Studies of satellite navigation

Research on satellite navigation has revealed some [18] patterns. A study in Canada found that people who used GPS the most had the weakest spatial memory, and that those who increased their use of it experienced a more [19] decline.

In a study in Japan, people who used paper maps drew more [20] sketches of their route than people who followed directions on a device. The device users could recall only [21] details, and lacked an [22] picture of how places were connected.

Questions 27-32

Reading Passage 3 has six sections, A-F.

Choose the correct heading for each section from the list of headings below.

Write the correct number, i-viii, in boxes 27-32 on your answer sheet.

List of Headings
i   A growing division in opinions
ii   Why people feel safer with familiar food
iii   The possible advantages of a new way of producing meat
iv   The rising cost of conventional meat
v   The benefits of letting consumers make decisions
vi   A launch that failed to win over the public
vii   Being open about the production process
viii   An unexpectedly popular new product

Questions 36-40

Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

In boxes 36-40 on your answer sheet, write

YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

questions.explanation: Answer: stairways 'On steep slopes, builders cut stairways into the rock'.
Answer: walls 'they built retaining walls to prevent the road from sliding down the hillside'.
Answer: channels ' channels were cut alongside them to carry rainwater away'.
Answer: cables Cords were braided 'to make thick cables '; 'The main cables were stretched across the gorge'.
Answer: branches ' Branches were then laid across the lowest cables to form a floor'.
Answer: year Grass rots, so 'each bridge had to be replaced regularly, usually every year '.
Answer: FALSE 'The roads were not open to everyone.' ' Ordinary people needed official permission to travel on them. '
Answer: NOT GIVEN The passage explains how chasquis carried messages, but not how they were chosen.
Answer: FALSE ' Since the Inca had no system of writing , runners either memorised spoken messages or carried quipus'.
Answer: TRUE ' the roads allowed their small army to move quickly through the empire, contributing to its rapid defeat '.

questions.correctAnswer: apurímac / apurimac / the apurímac / the apurimac / apurímac river / apurimac river
questions.explanation: Answer: Apurímac Q'eswachaka 'crosses the Apurímac River in southern Peru'.
Answer: June The bridge 'is still rebuilt every June by four local communities'.
Answer: Machu Picchu Visitors can walk 'the trail that leads to Machu Picchu '.

text.en: Our use of navigation technology may be affecting us in ways we do not notice.
Paper maps are more reliable than phones in unfamiliar cities.
Drivers depend on satellite navigation more than people on foot.
Few people know how to ask for directions any more.

questions.explanation: Answer: A ' But something less obvious is happening too : the parts of the brain that we once relied on to find our way are being used less and less'.

text.en: They have made people less willing to travel.
We should consider what they take away from us.
They are usually adopted too quickly.
Their benefits are often exaggerated.

questions.explanation: Answer: B ' the danger does not lie in adopting new tools, but in failing to ask what those tools are doing on our behalf that we used to do for ourselves '.

text.en: The ability to navigate is mainly inherited.
Simulated cities are useful for teaching navigation.
Following directions requires more effort than planning a route.
The brain changes according to how much it is used for a task.

questions.explanation: Answer: D The navigation system ' responds to the demands that are placed on it ', and 'the brain adapts accordingly'. It is not present at birth in its finished form (A).

text.en: They refuse to go out without their phones.
They lack basic skills of observation.
They become anxious in the mountains.
They do not listen to his instructions.

questions.explanation: Answer: B He is less worried by their anxiety (C) than by the fact that ' many of them have simply never learned to notice landmarks, to estimate distances or to keep track of the position of the sun '.
Answer: D (worrying) ' the pattern is certainly a worrying one '.
Answer: H (rapid) ' those whose GPS use had increased showed a faster decline ' – a more rapid decline.
Answer: F (accurate) ' the map users produced much more accurate drawings '.
Answer: B (isolated) Device users ' tended to remember isolated details , such as a particular shop or a café'.
Answer: C (overall) ' without any overall picture of how these places were connected '.
Answer: YES ' the way we travel also shapes what we notice and remember about the places we pass through '.
Answer: NO 'It applies to all of us, whatever our age: older adults are just as likely to lose these skills through lack of use as the young people Reilly describes '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The writer suggests 'studying a map before setting out', but gives no view on teaching map reading in schools.
Answer: YES The changes 'are not yet fixed, and we still have every opportunity to reverse them '.
Answer: iii Section A sets out the potential benefits: cultivated meat ' could require far less land and water than conventional farming and generate lower greenhouse gas emissions '.
Answer: vi The tasting events ' attracted a great deal of publicity, but not the kind the company had hoped for ', and the remaining events were cancelled.
Answer: ii ' Trust in food is based largely on familiarity and tradition ' – familiar food gives us 'a sense of security'.
Answer: i Films pushed people further in the direction they leaned, and ' society could divide into those who welcome it and those who reject it outright '.
Answer: vii ' Another approach is greater openness about how the meat is made. ' – open days and published ingredient lists.
Answer: v ' giving consumers a sense of control can improve acceptance ' – e.g. deciding how much cultivated meat goes into a burger.

text.en: proposing a solution to a problem
defending a controversial opinion
drawing attention to a difficulty
describing the history of a product

questions.explanation: Answer: C After the benefits, the writer highlights a problem: ' many consumers remain deeply reluctant to try it ', and says 'we need to understand where this reluctance comes from'.

text.en: They believe it is less nutritious than ordinary meat.
The way it is made is hard for them to imagine.
They would prefer to wait until it has been tested for longer.
They think it will harm traditional farmers.

questions.explanation: Answer: B Cultivated meat ' is made in a way that most people find very hard to picture '.

text.en: It encourages the public to see new foods as risky.
It pays too much attention to cultivated meat.
Its reports about food technology are usually inaccurate.
It blames scientists for food scares.

questions.explanation: Answer: A Food scares get disproportionate coverage and ' reinforce the message that anything new on our plates is likely to be risky '.
Answer: NO The films did not change people's minds: ' the effect was to push people further in the direction in which they already leaned '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The writer says cultivated meat will receive more attention, but makes no prediction about whether coverage will become more positive.
Answer: YES ' refusing even to consider it could leave many people worse off '.
Answer: NO 'Simply having tried an unfamiliar food appears to help': ' participants who had previously eaten plant-based meat substitutes were noticeably more open '.
Answer: YES Shoppers who could decide the mix rated the burger more highly, and ' if they feel they have some say in what they are eating, they will be far more willing ' to accept it.
